klein.name: Felix Christian Klein
klein.role: German Geometer, Group Theorist & Architect of the Göttingen School
klein.bio: Professor of Mathematics at Erlangen (1872), Munich, Leipzig, and Göttingen (from 1886). Formulated the Erlangen Program (Vergleichende Betrachtungen über neuere geometrische Forschungen, 1872), classifying every geometry as the invariant theory of a transformation group, unified non-Euclidean metrics under Cayley's projective Absolute (1871–1873), and delivered the 1895 Göttingen lectures on Famous Problems of Elementary Geometry synthesizing Gauss-Wantzel constructibility with Hermite-Lindemann-Gordan transcendence proofs.

taegert.name: Friedrich Tägert
taegert.bio: Prepared the authorized German redaction of Felix Klein's Göttingen Easter 1895 lecture notes, Vorträge über ausgewählte Fragen der Elementargeometrie (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1895), for the Elberfeld meeting.

beman.name: Wooster Woodruff Beman
beman.bio: Co-translator, with David Eugene Smith, of the authorized 1897 Ginn & Company English edition of Klein's Famous Problems of Elementary Geometry, as well as Dedekind's Essays on the Theory of Numbers.

smith.name: David Eugene Smith
smith.bio: Professor at Michigan State Normal School and later Teachers College, Columbia University; co-translator with W. W. Beman of Klein's Famous Problems of Elementary Geometry (1897).

haskell.name: Mellen Woodman Haskell
haskell.role: American Mathematician (UC Berkeley) & Doctoral Student of Klein
haskell.bio: Studied under Felix Klein at Göttingen and published the authorized 1893 English translation of the Erlangen Program ('A Comparative Review of Recent Researches in Geometry') in the Bulletin of the New York Mathematical Society.

gauss.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
gauss.bio: Discovered the compass-and-straightedge constructibility of the regular 17-gon on 30 March 1796 and proved in Section VII of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) that cyclotomic division into p = 2^(2^mu) + 1 parts reduces to a chain of quadratic period equations; also pioneered intrinsic surface curvature (1827).

wantzel.name: Pierre Laurent Wantzel
wantzel.bio: Published in Liouville's Journal (1837) the first complete algebraic impossibility proofs for duplicating the cube, trisecting a general angle, and constructing regular polygons whose odd prime divisors are not distinct Fermat primes.

galois.name: Évariste Galois
galois.role: French Mathematician, Founder of Galois Theory
galois.bio: Linked polynomial solvability by radicals to permutation groups of roots. In § 10 of the Erlangen Program, Klein explicitly parallels his group-theoretic classification of geometry with Galois's group theory of algebraic equations.

abel.name: Niels Henrik Abel
abel.bio: Proved the algebraic insolvability of the general quintic by radicals and characterized abelian (commutative-group) equations generalizing Gauss's cyclotomic periods.

eisenstein.name: Ferdinand Gotthold Max Eisenstein
eisenstein.bio: Formulated Eisenstein's irreducibility criterion (Crelle's Journal 39, 1850), deployed by Klein in Famous Problems Part I, Ch. III (§§ 7–8) to prove irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials of prime and prime-power order.

richelot.name: Friedrich Julius Richelot
richelot.bio: Carried out the explicit algebraic and geometric analysis for the regular 257-gon (p = 2^(2^3) + 1 = 257) in Crelle's Journal IX (1832), cited by Klein in Part I, Ch. III, § 1.

hermes.name: Johann Gustav Hermes
hermes.bio: Devoted ten years to the explicit period reduction of the regular 65537-gon (p = 2^(2^4) + 1 = 65537), depositing his manuscript trunk in the Göttingen Mathematical Seminary (Göttinger Nachrichten, 1894).

bachmann.name: Paul Gustav Heinrich Bachmann
bachmann.bio: Author of Die Lehre von der Kreistheilung (1872), cited by Klein as the standard treatise on cyclotomy and primitive-root period decompositions.

petersen.name: Julius Peter Christian Petersen
petersen.bio: Author of Methods and Theories for the Solution of Problems of Geometrical Constructions (1866/1879) and Theorie der algebraischen Gleichungen (1878); singled out by Klein in the Introduction to Famous Problems as virtually the sole textbook author presenting elementary impossibility proofs.

lemoine.name: Émile Michel Hyacinthe Lemoine
lemoine.bio: Formulated Géométrographie (1888–1902), quantifying operational simplicity and exactitude of ruler-and-compass vs. restricted-instrument constructions across the Euclidean canon.

mascheroni.name: Lorenzo Mascheroni
mascheroni.bio: Proved in La Geometria del Compasso (Pavia, 1797) that every point constructible with straightedge and compasses can be constructed with compasses alone.

poncelet.name: Jean-Victor Poncelet
poncelet.role: French Geometer & Engineer, Revivalist of Projective Geometry
poncelet.bio: Author of Traité des propriétés projectives des figures (1822); introduced ideal elements, circular points at infinity, homology, and first conceived straightedge constructions aided by a single fixed circle.

steiner.name: Jakob Steiner
steiner.bio: Proved in Die geometrischen Konstruktionen, ausgeführt mittelst der geraden Linie und eines festen Kreises (1833) that every ruler-and-compass construction can be executed with a straightedge alone once a single fixed circle and its center are given.

staudt.name: Karl Georg Christian von Staudt
staudt.bio: Published the fixed-circle straightedge construction of the regular 17-gon (Crelle's Journal 24, 1842) and founded metric-free synthetic projective geometry in Geometrie der Lage (1847) and Beiträge zur Geometrie der Lage (1856–1860), including geometric 'throws' (Würfe) and imaginary elements.

schroeter.name: Heinrich Eduard Schröter
schroeter.bio: Recast and simplified von Staudt's single-circle straightedge construction of the regular 17-gon in Crelle's Journal 75 (1872), directly adapted by Klein in Famous Problems Part I, Ch. IV (§§ 8–9).

lambert.name: Johann Heinrich Lambert
lambert.bio: Pioneered perspective straightedge constructions in Freie Perspective (1774), investigated the parallel postulate, and proved the irrationality of pi via continued fractions in 1761/1770 (Part II, Ch. II, § 4).

brianchon.name: Charles Julien Brianchon
brianchon.bio: Discovered the dual of Pascal's hexagram theorem and investigated pure straightedge constructions (1818), cited by Klein in Part I, Ch. IV, § 7.

wiener.name: Hermann Ludwig Gustav Wiener
wiener.bio: Demonstrated regular polygon constructions by paper folding (noted in Dyck's 1893 Munich Mathematical Exhibition Catalogue) and lectured on foundational incidence axioms anticipating Hilbert.

sundara-row.name: T. Sundara Row (Rao)
sundara-row.bio: Author of Geometrical Exercises in Paper Folding (Madras: Addison & Co., 1893), commended by Klein in Famous Problems Part I, Ch. V, § 1, triggering international interest in origami geometry.

diocles.name: Diocles
diocles.bio: Author of On Burning Mirrors; invented the cubic cissoid (x^2 + y^2)x - y^2 = 0 to solve the Delian duplication of the cube (Famous Problems Part I, Ch. V, § 3).

nicomedes.name: Nicomedes
nicomedes.bio: Invented the quartic conchoid (x^2 + y^2)(x - a)^2 - b^2 x^2 = 0 and a mechanical trammel to trisect arbitrary angles and duplicate the cube via neusis (Famous Problems Part I, Ch. V, §§ 4–5).

hippias.name: Hippias of Elis
hippias.bio: Discovered the transcendental quadratrix curve y/x = tan(pi*y/2) for angle multisection, later applied by Dinostratus (c. 350 BC) to rectify and square the circle (Part II, Ch. II, § 2).

archimedes.name: Archimedes of Syracuse
archimedes.bio: Bounded pi rigorously between 3 + 10/71 and 3 + 1/7 via inscribed and circumscribed 96-gons in Measurement of a Circle (Part II, Ch. II, § 2).

euclid.name: Euclid of Alexandria
euclid.role: Greek Geometer, Author of the Elements
euclid.bio: Codified compass-and-straightedge geometry (Postulates 1–3) and regular 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 15-gon constructions in Book IV of the Elements, setting the classical canon analyzed by Gauss and Klein.

pappus.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus.bio: Classified geometric problems in Synagoge Books III–IV into plane (straightedge & compass), solid (conic sections), and linear (higher curves), and proved projective cross-ratio invariance in Book VII.

kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
kepler.bio: Argued in Harmonices Mundi Book I (1619) that the regular heptagon (n = 7) is 'unknowable' (inscibilis) because its chord ratio satisfies a solid (cubic) equation ungrounded in planar Euclidean bisections—rigorously vindicated by Gauss, Wantzel, and Klein.

huygens.name: Christiaan Huygens
huygens.bio: Refined Archimedean polygon bounds in De circuli magnitudine inventa (1654), obtaining dramatically sharper rational enclosures for pi (Part II, Ch. II, § 2).

leibniz.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
leibniz.bio: Discovered the alternating arctangent series for pi/4, introduced the distinction between algebraic, transcendental, and 'interscendental' expressions (Part II, Ch. IV, § 1), and envisioned geometry of situation (analysis situs).

euler.name: Leonhard Euler
euler.bio: Established the analytic nexus e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0 between exponential and circular functions (Introductio in analysin infinitorum, 1748), enabling Lindemann's 1882 deduction of the transcendence of pi from exponential independence.

legendre.name: Adrien-Marie Legendre
legendre.bio: Proved the irrationality of both pi and pi^2 in Éléments de géométrie (1794) and conjectured the existence of non-algebraic (transcendental) numbers (Part II, Ch. II, § 4).

liouville.name: Joseph Liouville
liouville.bio: Constructed the first provably transcendental numbers in 1844/1851 via Diophantine rational-approximation bounds, and proved in 3-space that conformal transformations reduce to the Möbius group of inversions (Erlangen § 6).

cantor.name: Georg Cantor
cantor.role: German Mathematician, Creator of Transfinite Set Theory
cantor.bio: Proved in 1873/1874 (Crelle 77) and via his 1891 diagonal method that algebraic numbers are countable whereas the continuum is uncountable, establishing the ubiquity of transcendental numbers (Famous Problems Part II, Ch. I).

hermite.name: Charles Hermite
hermite.bio: Proved the transcendence of Euler's constant e in 1873 (Comptes Rendus, 'Sur la fonction exponentielle'), opening the modern analytical theory of transcendence.

lindemann.name: Carl Louis Ferdinand von Lindemann
lindemann.role: German Mathematician & Doctoral Student of Klein
lindemann.bio: Earned his doctorate under Felix Klein at Erlangen (1873) on non-Euclidean mechanics and proved in June 1882 ('Über die Zahl π', Mathematische Annalen 20) the transcendence of pi, settling the 2,300-year problem of squaring the circle.

weierstrass.name: Karl Theodor Wilhelm Weierstrass
weierstrass.bio: Simplified and generalized the Hermite–Lindemann theorem in the Berlin Sitzungsberichte (1885), establishing algebraic independence of exponentials for distinct algebraic exponents.

gordan.name: Paul Albert Gordan
gordan.bio: Klein's colleague at Erlangen who in 1893 (Mathematische Annalen 43) eliminated definite integrals from the proofs of Hermite and Lindemann via symbolic factorial operators h^r = r!, forming the direct basis of Famous Problems Part II, Chs. III–IV.

hilbert.name: David Hilbert
hilbert.bio: Klein's colleague at Göttingen from 1895; published a celebrated 1893 simplification of the transcendence of e and pi (Mathematische Annalen 43) and in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899) Ch. VII refined segment constructibility under gauge-compass axioms.

hurwitz.name: Adolf Hurwitz
hurwitz.role: German Mathematician & Doctoral Student of Klein
hurwitz.bio: Published an elementary mean-value modification of Hilbert's transcendence proof for e in Göttinger Nachrichten / Mathematische Annalen 43 (1893).

rudio.name: Ferdinand Rudio
rudio.bio: Published Archimedes, Huygens, Lambert, Legendre: Vier Abhandlungen über die Kreismessung (Leipzig: Teubner, 1892), whose historical synthesis Klein follows throughout Famous Problems Part II, Ch. II.

abakanowicz.name: Bruno Abdank-Abakanowicz
abakanowicz.bio: Invented the mechanical integraph (Les intégraphes, Paris, 1886; German ed. by Bitterli, 1889, built by G. Coradi of Zürich), demonstrated by Klein in Famous Problems Part II, Ch. V / Anhang to construct pi via continuous curve integration.

lie.name: Marius Sophus Lie
lie.role: Norwegian Mathematician, Founder of Continuous Transformation Groups
lie.bio: Klein's closest collaborator during 1869–1872 in Berlin and Paris; discovered contact transformations and Lie's sphere geometry mapping lines into spheres (§§ 7 & 9 of the Erlangen Program) and co-inspired Klein's group-theoretic synthesis.

cayley.name: Arthur Cayley
cayley.bio: Showed in his Sixth Memoir upon Quantics (1859) that Euclidean metric geometry is a special projective invariant theory relative to an Absolute conic/quadric ('metrical geometry is a part of descriptive geometry'), generalized to non-Euclidean spaces by Klein (1871–1872).

riemann.name: Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann
riemann.bio: Introduced n-dimensional manifolds (Mannigfaltigkeiten), conformal complex mappings, analysis situs, and quadratic differential curvature in his 1854 Habilitationsvortrag (published 1867), synthesized with projective group theory in § 10 and Notes IV–VI of Klein's Erlangen Program.

helmholtz.name: Hermann von Helmholtz
helmholtz.bio: Characterized constant-curvature Riemannian metrics via free mobility of rigid bodies (1868), connected by Klein and Lie to transitive continuous transformation groups.

pluecker.name: Julius Plücker
pluecker.role: German Geometer & Physicist,Klein's Mentor at Bonn
pluecker.bio: Klein's teacher at Bonn whose Neue Geometrie des Raumes (completed by Klein, 1868–1869) elevated the straight line in 3-space to a primary 4-dimensional space-element on a quadric in P^5 (Erlangen § 5).

moebius.name: August Ferdinand Möbius
moebius.bio: Classified hierarchy of geometric affinities—congruence, similarity, affinity, and collineation—in Der barycentrische Calcul (1827) and developed the Kreisverwandtschaft (circular/inversion transformations, 1855) generalized in Erlangen §§ 1–2 & § 6.

chasles.name: Michel Chasles
chasles.bio: Systematized cross-ratio (rapport anharmonique), homography, duality, and enumerative characteristics across Aperçu historique (1837) and Traité de géométrie supérieure (1852).

hesse.name: Ludwig Otto Hesse
hesse.bio: Formulated Hesse's Principle of Transference (Übertragungsprincip, 1866) mapping binary projective forms onto points of a conic or twisted cubic, highlighted by Klein as a model of group equivalence in Erlangen §§ 4–5.

clebsch.name: Rudolf Friedrich Alfred Clebsch
clebsch.bio: Klein's mentor at Göttingen and co-founder of Mathematische Annalen, who championed algebraic invariant theory and birational geometry before his untimely death in November 1872 just as Klein entered Erlangen.

cremona.name: Luigi Cremona
cremona.bio: Developed the theory of birational (Cremona) transformations of the plane and 3-space, examined as an infinite-parameter algebraic group in § 8.1 of the Erlangen Program.

grassmann.name: Hermann Günther Grassmann
grassmann.role: German Polymath, Creator of Exterior Algebra
grassmann.bio: Pioneered n-dimensional linear and affine extension theory in Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre (1844, 1862), cited by Klein in § 10.3 and Note III on manifolds.

beltrami.name: Eugenio Beltrami
beltrami.bio: Modeled hyperbolic geometry on pseudospherical surfaces and geodesic projective disks (1868) and studied conformal invariants in higher dimensions (Erlangen § 6 & Note V).

lobatchewsky.name: Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky
lobatchewsky.role: Russian Geometer, Co-Founder of Hyperbolic Geometry
lobatchewsky.bio: Published the first non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) synthetic geometry (1829–1840), identified by Klein in 1871 and Erlangen Note V with projective geometry inside a real non-degenerate Absolute quadric.

bolyai.name: János Bolyai
bolyai.role: Hungarian Mathematician, Co-Founder of Hyperbolic Geometry
bolyai.bio: Author of the 1832 Appendix developing absolute and hyperbolic geometry independently of Lobachevsky (Erlangen Note V).

russell.name: Bertrand Arthur William Russell
russell.bio: Adopted Klein's Cayley–Klein projective hierarchy and transformation-group classification as the mathematical backbone of An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897) and Part VI of The Principles of Mathematics (1903).

hoenen.name: Petrus Hubertus Jacobus Hoenen, S.J.
hoenen.bio: Critically analyzed Klein's Erlangen Program, Cayley–Klein models, and axiomatic structuralism in De Noetica Geometriae (1954), distinguishing formal group isomorphism from intuitive spatial abstraction.

wildberger.name: Norman John Wildberger
wildberger.role: Canadian-Australian Mathematician, Creator of Rational Trigonometry
wildberger.bio: Replaced transcendental distance and angle by algebraic quadrance Q and spread s in Divine Proportions (2005) and Universal Hyperbolic Geometry, providing polynomial invariants over arbitrary fields directly realizing Klein's algebraic Erlangen program.
